name: cdecl
desc: Turn English phrases to C or C++ declarations
why: Translates English phrases into C declarations, a charming old-school tool that makes pointer-soup readable.

brief.what_it_is: cdecl is a command-line program for composing and deciphering C or C++ declarations and casts. You type an English phrase such as "declare p as pointer to const pointer to const char" and it prints the C declaration, or you give it a C declaration and it explains it in English. It runs interactively on a terminal or takes input from the command line or standard input. It also has a mode for developing and debugging C preprocessor macros by showing each expansion step. The installed executables are cdecl and c++decl.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the problem as C declaration syntax, which mirrors how the variables are used and draws strong criticism; it quotes Dennis Ritchie and Bjarne Stroustrup on that point. cdecl exists to make that "gibberish" readable and writable.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not describe the internals beyond saying it uses flex and bison for the lexer and parser (the parser is parser.y and the lexer is lexer.l). It supports many language standards, from K&R C through C23 and C++98 through C++26, and it can be used interactively or non-interactively.

brief.install_notes: The git repository does not include configure, so building from source needs autoconf, automake, and m4 to run ./bootstrap, plus flex and bison (lex and yacc are not sufficient). Alternatively, download a released version from the GitHub releases page, which includes configure and the generated lexer and parser; then follow the generic INSTALL instructions. Coverage reports need gcov (from gcc) and lcov. Developer docs need Doxygen. Native Windows is not supported; the README suggests Cygwin, MinGW-64, or WSL. No accounts or runtime services are mentioned.
brief.standout: Its main claim is that it is the most complete and current implementation of this English-to-C-declaration tool. It covers many standards, including C++20 and C++23 features and Windows calling conventions, and it has a macro-expansion stepper that goes beyond declaration translation. The README also includes a detailed licensing history for the code.
brief.status: Appears maintained. The README is dated 13 June 2024 and describes versions 3.0 and later under GPL v3. I did not check the releases or commit history, so the latest release date and last commit are unknown.
brief.caveats: Licensing is unusual. The original code from the mid-1980s by Graham Ross never had a copyright notice or license. The author states that cdecl 3.0 and later are under GPL v3, relies on a public-domain argument and a fair-use analysis for the older code, and disclaims being a lawyer. The project only runs on Unix-like systems because it uses Autotools. Native Windows is not supported. Building from git requires extra tools (autoconf, automake, m4, flex, bison). The README says the GitHub repository is the only official site for 3.0 and later. The Homebrew entry lists no caveats.

judge.reason: A lesser-known two-way translator for C’s famously tangled declarations, with an unexpectedly useful step-by-step preprocessor macro expander.

entry.title: cdecl
entry.tldr: Turns English like "pointer to const pointer to const char" into a C or C++ declaration, and explains declarations back in English.
entry.deeper_look:
cdecl is a command-line translator for C and C++ declarations and casts. Type `declare p as pointer to const pointer to const char` and it prints `const char *const *p;`. Give it `int *const (*p)[4]` with `explain` and it answers "declare p as pointer to array 4 of constant pointer to integer". It runs as an interactive prompt, or reads from the command line or standard input.

The reason it exists is the declaration syntax itself. C declarations mirror how a variable is used, which makes them hard to read. The README quotes Dennis Ritchie saying he is "still uncertain" about that design, and Bjarne Stroustrup calling it "an experiment that failed". cdecl is the tool for the gibberish those choices produce.

The idea underneath is that C declarations are a small grammar you can learn to parse by hand, and a tool that does it for you shows the rules at work. The code is built on a flex lexer and a bison parser. This version covers standards from K&R C through C23 and C++98 through C++26.

It also has a mode for debugging preprocessor macros. Define a macro inside the session, run `expand` on a use of it, and cdecl shows each substitution step. That goes beyond declaration translation, and it is useful for token-pasting tricks like `A ## B`.
entry.install:
brew install cdecl
# installs two executables: cdecl and c++decl
